questions.q: What question does performance tuning ask, given a query is already correct?
options: How do you make it run faster or use fewer resources while returning the exact same result?
How do you make it return different rows?
How do you add more columns to the output?
How do you rewrite it using only JOIN, never subqueries?
questions.explain: Performance tuning is a separate concern from correctness — the result set must stay identical.

questions.q: Why can a query that runs fine on a 1,000-row test table become a real problem in production?
options: A query that doesn't scale well can take minutes instead of milliseconds against a much larger table
Test tables always run faster than production tables regardless of query design
Production tables use a different SQL dialect
This scenario never actually happens in practice
questions.explain: This is exactly why performance tuning becomes increasingly valuable as databases grow to real scale.

questions.q: How does this chapter differ from earlier chapters in this course?
options: It focuses on comparisons between different ways to write the same correct query, rather than introducing new syntax
It introduces entirely new SQL keywords not covered anywhere else
It focuses exclusively on SELECT statements with no WHERE clauses
It requires a different database than AdventureWorks2012
questions.explain: Joins vs. subqueries, EXISTS vs. IN, clustered vs. nonclustered indexes — these are comparisons of equivalent-result approaches.

questions.q: What makes the comparisons in this chapter (like joins vs. subqueries) meaningful?
options: Both approaches can produce identical results — the difference is entirely in how SQL Server has to work to get there
Only one of the two approaches ever returns correct results
They only apply to SELECT DISTINCT queries
They are purely stylistic with no actual performance difference
questions.explain: The whole premise of performance tuning here is comparing equally-correct approaches for their actual cost.

questions.q: What topics does this lesson preview for the rest of Chapter 10?
options: Cartesian products, joins vs. subqueries, indexes, execution plans, and common anti-patterns
Only stored procedures and dynamic SQL
Only data warehouse concepts
Only transactions and locking
questions.explain: This lesson maps out the chapter's full scope, tying back to real comparative performance questions.
